note: Episodes written for the C1 and F1 lessons, placed in the chapters MASTER_PLAN.md assigns them by language focus. Season 1 is six chapters of two episodes each; see story.ledger.json for what is written and what is not. Every episode here is draft: not challenged, not reviewed, not integrated, not pilot-approved.

episodes.title: The Letter’s Recipient
episodes.intro: The port file gives up a letter at last, and it is almost useless. The writer never names anybody. She writes that she gave it to her, that he had promised them, that they would know what to do. Every sentence is clear to the two people who already knew what had happened, and to nobody since. Somewhere in this tangle is the person the letter was meant for. To find them you have to work out which pronoun is standing in for which name.
episodes.recap: You traced every pronoun in the letter back to the person it stood for, and found that one of them could not mean who everyone assumed. The letter was written to a sister, not to a Mr.
episodes.problem: The letter uses pronouns without naming anyone, so its recipient is unclear.
episodes.decision: Decide which name each pronoun replaces, using its form and its position, rather than assuming the obvious reading.
episodes.consequence: One pronoun turns out to be doing the work of a subject where everyone had read an object, which changes who was acting.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: If the letter was meant for a sister, why does the cover name a man?
episodes.reveal: A pronoun is only as clear as the name behind it. She and her are not interchangeable: one does the action and one receives it, and swapping them reverses who did what. Reading the forms carefully turns an unreadable letter into a straightforward one, and points at a cover that does not match its contents.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: The National Archives keeps passenger records for people who left British ports. It also explains how those records are indexed. The British Library holds papers about printing in Britain. Invented: this letter, its writer, the port file, and the name on the cover. Uncertain: letters like this often relied on what the writer and reader both knew. Much of that is now lost.

episodes.title: The Name on the Cover
episodes.intro: The letter inside was written to a sister, but the cover names a man. Both of those facts sit on the same piece of paper. Only one of them can describe the person who was meant to open it. The clerk who addressed the cover used a comma in one place and left it out in another. That single mark is the whole of the difference. One version hands the letter to Mr Ames as its owner. The other asks him to pass it along.
episodes.recap: You read the cover twice, once with the comma and once without it, and the mark decided everything. With the comma the name belongs to somebody being spoken to, and without it the same name becomes the person who owns the letter.
episodes.problem: The cover names a man, although the letter folded inside it was clearly written to a woman.
episodes.decision: Work out whether the name on the cover is being addressed or being named as the owner.
episodes.consequence: The comma shows the clerk was asking Mr Ames to pass the letter along. He was never meant to read it.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: If he was only passing it on, why did the letter stay in his papers for forty years?
episodes.reveal: A comma placed before a name changes who the sentence is about. Speaking to somebody separates their name from whatever you are saying to them, and naming them as the owner does not. The clerk understood that difference, and so did everyone who handled the letter while it still mattered. The meaning was lost much later, when the cover was copied out by hand and the comma went missing.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: The National Archives keeps passenger records for people who left British ports. It also explains how to search them. The comma rule for speaking to someone by name is standard English. The Language Portal of Canada sets it out. Invented: this letter, its cover, the clerk, and Mr Ames. Uncertain: old covers were often copied by hand. Small marks were lost that way. We rarely know when.

episodes.title: Two Accounts
episodes.intro: Two people wrote down what happened that winter, and the accounts do not agree. Worse, generations of readers have added their conclusions in the margins until it is impossible to tell the record from the reading. One note says the family left in a hurry. Another says the barn was already gone. Neither account says either of those things. Before you can decide which version to believe, you have to strip the file back to what it actually states.
episodes.recap: You sorted every claim in the file into what the documents state and what earlier readers had concluded. Two of the four margin notes turned out to rest on nothing at all.
episodes.problem: Earlier readers wrote their conclusions into the file as though the documents had said them.
episodes.decision: Sort every claim into stated or worked out before trusting any of it.
episodes.consequence: Stripped of the additions, the two accounts disagree about far less than anyone thought.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: Who added the margin notes, and did they know something the file no longer holds?
episodes.reveal: The accounts never contradicted each other. What contradicted them was a century of readers writing conclusions in pencil and later readers mistaking those for the record. A conclusion you can trace back to a sentence is worth keeping. One you cannot is somebody else’s guess wearing the clothes of a fact.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: Library and Archives Canada describes land settlement records for immigrants. It says what those records hold. The Provincial Archives of Alberta publishes search tools for its own holdings. Invented: this file, the two accounts, the margin notes, and the family. Uncertain: real files often do carry notes from earlier readers. Telling a note from the record is a real difficulty, not a trick of the story.

episodes.title: What the Words Were Worth
episodes.intro: With the margin notes gone, the accounts still hold more than they say. One mentions a kettle still warm. The other describes the ink as fugitive and the neighbour as reticent, words you cannot look up here. Nothing states who was in the house or what the neighbour knew. But the details are not random, and the writer could not help explaining his hard words as he went. What is left is a case built from what the pages imply.
episodes.recap: You drew conclusions the accounts supported without stating, and worked out four unfamiliar words from the sentences around them. A warm kettle and a reticent neighbour turned out to be the same clue.
episodes.problem: The accounts imply more than they state, and use words the investigator does not know.
episodes.decision: Build each conclusion on a detail you can point to, and read each unfamiliar word from what surrounds it.
episodes.consequence: The neighbour was present and unwilling to say so, which gives the case a witness nobody had counted.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: What did the neighbour see that was worth staying quiet about?
episodes.reveal: Fugitive did not mean a person fleeing. The sentence explained it: ink that fades in sunlight and vanishes within a year. A word carries a different meaning in a different trade, and the sentence around it tells you which. The same reading gave you the neighbour: a warm kettle nobody mentioned, and a man who would not discuss the evening.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: Library and Archives Canada explains how to find old newspapers. It also describes land settlement records for immigrants. Invented: these two accounts, the neighbour, the kettle, and every word quoted here. Uncertain: trade words of the time were not fixed. The same word could mean one thing in one district and something else nearby.

episodes.title: What the Witness Actually Said
episodes.intro: The newspaper office keeps two copies of the same report. One is the reporter’s notebook and one was set into print. They say noticeably different things, and nobody moved a single word between them. In the notebook the witness is quoted directly. In the printed version the quotation marks have vanished. What she said has become what the paper reports as having happened. Those are not the same claim, and only one of them can be checked against her.
episodes.recap: Comparing the notebook against the printed page showed that the quotation marks had gone missing somewhere between them. Her exact words had become the newspaper’s own statement, so nobody could hold her to them afterwards.
episodes.problem: A quotation lost its marks somewhere in printing, so a witness statement now reads as established fact.
episodes.decision: Work out which words the witness actually spoke, and mark them as hers.
episodes.consequence: Restoring the marks puts the claim back in her mouth, where it can be questioned.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: Was the printer careless, or did somebody want the claim to look settled?
episodes.reveal: Quotation marks are a promise about accuracy. The words inside them are exactly what somebody said, and the words outside them belong to whoever is writing. Dropping the marks moves a claim from one person to another without altering a single letter. A reader coming to the page fresh has no way of telling that it happened.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: Library and Archives Canada holds Canadian newspapers. It explains how to search them. The rules for punctuating speech are standard English. Invented: this newspaper, the reporter, the witness, and both copies of the report. Uncertain: printers did make errors like this one. Whether any single error was on purpose is almost never possible to show.

episodes.title: Two Sentences Pushed Together
episodes.intro: There is a second difference between the notebook and the printed page, and it is easier to miss. The reporter wrote two short sentences. The printed version runs them together with nothing but a comma between them. Read the line quickly and nothing seems wrong at all. Read it as a single sentence and the second half becomes the reason for the first. The reporter never wrote down any reason at all.
episodes.recap: Separating the two statements showed that neither one of them actually explained the other. Joined together by a single comma, the second of them had looked very much like a cause.
episodes.problem: Two separate statements were joined by a single comma, which made the second look like the cause of the first.
episodes.decision: Decide where each complete statement ends, and separate them properly.
episodes.consequence: Apart, the two facts sit side by side. Nothing in the notebook says one led to the other.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: The same hand made both changes. Did one person set this page?
episodes.reveal: A comma between two complete statements does considerably more than break a rule, because it suggests a link that the writer never claimed. A full stop leaves the two facts standing side by side, and the reader is then free to decide whether one of them explains the other. That decision belongs to the reader, and punctuation is quite capable of taking it away.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: Library and Archives Canada holds Canadian newspapers. It explains how to search them. The rule about joining two complete statements is standard English. The Language Portal of Canada sets it out. Invented: this newspaper, the reporter, and both versions of the report. Uncertain: we cannot know what a long-dead printer meant by one comma.

episodes.title: The Words on the Manifest
episodes.intro: The railway carried more than people, and the freight manifest proves it. Half the words on it are ones you have never met: unshipped, reconsigned, undeliverable, remeasurement. The clerk who wrote them is long dead and cannot explain himself. But none of these words is really new. Each is an ordinary word with something added to the front or the back, and each addition changes the meaning in a way you can predict. Take them apart and the manifest starts to speak.
episodes.recap: You broke the clerk’s long words into their parts and read a manifest nobody had understood in years. One word, reconsigned, tells you the crate was sent on somewhere else.
episodes.problem: The manifest is written in words built from parts, and nobody left a glossary.
episodes.decision: Work out each unfamiliar word from its base, its prefix and its suffix, instead of guessing from its shape.
episodes.consequence: Reconsigned means sent on to somebody else, which points at a destination nobody has looked for.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: If the crate was sent on, who signed for it at the other end?
episodes.reveal: The long words were never the obstacle. Unshipped is the base ship, with un- meaning not: it never went aboard. Reconsigned is consign with re- meaning again: it was sent a second time. Once you can take a word apart, you can read a page written by somebody who never expected you to see it.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: Library and Archives Canada describes land settlement records for immigrants. The National Archives keeps passenger and shipping records. It also explains how they are indexed. Invented: this manifest, the clerk, the crate, and every word on it. Uncertain: the wording of real freight papers changed from one company to the next. No single glossary would fit them all.

episodes.title: Names Nobody Can Say
episodes.intro: To follow the crate you need the station register, and the register is full of names. Not famous ones — ordinary names, written by hand, belonging to people nobody has looked for in a century. Nobody alive knows how to say them. The archivist watches you stall on one and says the thing that unlocks the rest of the work: you do not need to have heard a word to read it. You need to know what its letters usually do.
episodes.recap: You read a page of names nobody had spoken aloud in a hundred years, using the patterns the letters follow rather than memory. One of them matched a name on the manifest.
episodes.problem: The register is full of unfamiliar names and there is nobody left to pronounce them.
episodes.decision: Read each name by its patterns — what the vowels do, where the word breaks into beats — rather than waiting to recognise it.
episodes.consequence: The names become readable, and one matches the signature on the reconsigned crate.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: If the same name appears in both records, is it the same person or only the same spelling?
episodes.reveal: Every name on the page followed rules you already had. A silent e at the end reaches back and lengthens the vowel before it. Two consonants between vowels usually means the break falls between them. You will meet words nobody has ever said to you for the rest of your life, and this is how you read them anyway.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: The National Archives keeps passenger records. It explains how they are indexed and searched. The Provincial Archives of Alberta publishes search tools for its own holdings. Invented: this register, the archivist, and every name in it. Uncertain: one family name was often spelled several ways across records. A match in spelling is not by itself a match in person.

episodes.title: Reading for One Thing at a Time
episodes.intro: Every document in the case is laid out on the archive table at once. There is the manuscript, the printed proof, the letter, its cover, the notebook and the printed page. Somewhere across those six documents is the pattern that explains the whole business. Reading them for everything at once has already failed you twice. The archivist suggests something a good deal slower. Read all six of them for spelling alone, then read all six again for punctuation.
episodes.recap: Reading the whole case one kind of mistake at a time brought the pattern out on the second pass. Every single change turned out to be punctuation, and not one of them was a spelling error.
episodes.problem: Six documents hold changes of several different kinds, and reading for all of them at once keeps missing some.
episodes.decision: Read for one kind of mistake at a time, and record what each pass finds.
episodes.consequence: The punctuation pass finds changes in five of the six documents. The spelling pass finds nothing at all.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: Someone who changed only punctuation knew exactly what punctuation does. Who was that careful?
episodes.reveal: Looking for everything at once means your eye settles on the first thing it finds and stops noticing the rest. Looking for one thing at a time means that you actually finish the page. The pattern running through this case had stayed invisible for a straightforward reason. It was made of marks rather than words, and nobody had read the documents for marks alone.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: the Provincial Archives of Alberta publish search tools for their holdings. Library and Archives Canada holds land settlement records. Invented: this table of six documents, the archivist, and the case itself. Uncertain: archivists do read records in passes like this. The method here is made simpler to fit a story.

episodes.title: The Smallest Change That Puts It Right
episodes.intro: You know what was changed and you know exactly how it was done. That leaves the hardest part of the business still ahead of you. The attribution has to be corrected, and a correction can break as much as it mends. Change too little and the record carries on misleading everybody who reads it. Change too much and you have written your own version over somebody else’s. The archivist asks for the smallest change that puts it right, together with the evidence for it.
episodes.recap: You corrected the attribution with a single change and set out the six documents that support it. Everything else in the record was left exactly as you found it.
episodes.problem: The record is wrong, and a correction of it can easily change a good deal more than it should.
episodes.decision: Make the smallest change that puts the record right, and set out the evidence for it.
episodes.consequence: One name changes. Everything else stands, and every step can be traced back to a document.
episodes.unresolvedQuestion: The letter stayed in his papers for forty years. That part is still not explained.
episodes.reveal: A correction is itself a claim, and a claim of that kind needs evidence behind it. The smallest change is the honest one. Everything beyond it is your own reading rather than anything the record actually says. What you can show is the part that lasts. What you merely assumed is the part that somebody corrects after you.
episodes.historyBehindMystery: Documented: the Provincial Archives of Alberta publish search tools. The National Archives holds records about William Caxton. He set up the first printing press in England. Invented: this record, the change to it, and the archivist. Uncertain: archives do revise records when the evidence supports it. How often they do so varies from one to the next.
